interactions.summary: Jiang opens the session by warning that these final two Dante classes will be the most intense because the seminar will read line by line from Canto 24 through the end of the Divine Comedy.
A student jumps ahead to ask why Dante, while discussing faith in heaven, compares faith to a coin and the self to a purse.
Jiang says the class has not reached that passage yet, asks the student to wait, and invites another question.
Another student asks whether Dante's lines about priesthood, flesh, plunder, politics, and indolence amount to a critique of the Catholic Church and of selling mind, body, or salvation.
Jiang answers that Dante is indeed bluntly criticizing indulgences and the Church's use of paid penance reductions to finance projects like St. Peter's Basilica.

Jiang then sets the historical and emotional scene for the final cantos by placing Dante in exile near death, stripped of home, wealth, political standing, and certainty about how his work will be received.

speaker_notes.note: ASR mangles several proper nouns in Jiang's historical setup, but the intended frame is Dante's exile from Florence under pressure from Pope Boniface and hostile Florentine factions.

claims.claim: Jiang says the final two seminar meetings will cover Canto 24 through Canto 33 line by line because the end of the Divine Comedy demands unusually intense attention.
Jiang interprets Dante's critique of corruption as including the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences, where wealth can purchase reduced penance in purgatory.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive claim about Dante stated on 2026-06-18.

claims.claim: He says the Church used indulgence practices to finance projects such as St. Peter's Basilica.
Jiang argues that as the poem ascends into heaven, Dante's criticism of Church corruption becomes even more blatant rather than more conciliatory.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive claim about the poem's movement stated on 2026-06-18.

claims.claim: Jiang frames the last cantos as being written when Dante is near death, exiled from Florence, stripped of property, and uncertain whether posterity will honor the Divine Comedy or condemn it as heresy.

signature_moments.moment: Indulgences are rendered as the rich man's loophole for buying down punishment after a wicked life.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This sharpens Jiang's claim that Dante's anti-Church edge is financial and institutional, not just moralistic.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang asks the class to picture Dante as a patron-supported beggar finishing his masterpiece while cut off from home and threatened by Church power.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It sets the poem's ending inside extremity, despair, and reputational risk rather than inside stable literary triumph.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: A Church practice Jiang describes as letting wealthy sinners pay for reduced penance in purgatory.

chronology_notes.note: Jiang explicitly dates Dante's emotional position to the final one or two years before Dante's 1321 death and treats that late-life situation as crucial for reading the end of Paradiso.

uncertainty_notes.note: Several historical names are distorted by ASR, so preserve the larger exile-versus-papacy framing without overcommitting to every malformed proper noun.
